new.title: Slip into the courtyard of Hof van Liere
new.desc: Behind the gate of the university's city campus hides a Brabantine Gothic palace with a quiet inner garden. Students cross it on their way to class while most visitors walk right past.
new.tip: Use the main gate on Prinsstraat during the day; the side gate on Grote Kauwenberg is not always open.

new.title: Take a breather in Den Botaniek
new.desc: The city's small botanic garden packs a pond with a waterfall, statues, a greenhouse and herb beds into a walled pocket just off the busy shopping streets.
new.tip: Come with a sandwich at lunchtime; ten minutes on a bench here resets a whole afternoon of shopping.

new.title: Find the hidden Calvary of Sint-Paulus
new.desc: Next to Sint-Pauluskerk, an 18th-century artificial rock garden is crowded with 63 life-size statues of angels, prophets and evangelists climbing towards the cross. Inside the church hang works by Rubens and a row of carved Baroque confessionals.
new.tip: The Calvary is behind a door to the right of the church entrance; it is usually open in the afternoon, daily in summer and on weekends in winter.

new.title: Push open the door of the Keizerskapel
new.desc: The Sint-Annakapel on Keizerstraat looks like nothing from the street, but inside it is a richly decorated little chapel under a starry blue ceiling.
new.tip: Opening hours are erratic, so simply try the door when you pass; leave a coin in the donation box.

new.title: Step into the Nottebohmzaal library hall
new.desc: The Erfgoedbibliotheek Hendrik Conscience hides a two-storey 19th-century reading room full of old books, Blaeu globes and an Egyptian cabinet, named after the patron Oscar Nottebohm.
new.tip: The hall is mostly shown on guided tours or during events; check the library's agenda and book a slot before you go.

new.title: Hear the silence in the Begijnhof
new.desc: Behind a plain wall on Rodestraat lies the 16th-century beguinage: cobbled lanes, small brick houses and a walled garden that feels miles away from the student cafés on the Ossenmarkt next door.
new.tip: People still live here, so keep your voice down; dogs are not allowed.

new.title: Stand under the roof of the old Handelsbeurs
new.desc: Antwerp built one of the first purpose-built stock exchanges in the world in the 16th century. The neo-Gothic hall that replaced it after a fire has been beautifully restored, with its iron-and-glass roof and painted arches.
new.tip: Find the entrance in a side street off the Meir; the main hall is free to look around when it is open.

new.title: Have a coffee in the Stadsfeestzaal
new.desc: The city's old banquet hall on the Meir burned down in 2000 and came back as a shopping centre that kept its gilded neoclassical hall, balconies and glass roof.
new.tip: Head for the café upstairs and look down over the hall; it is a calm rainy-day stop between the Meir crowds.

new.title: Meet Lange Wapper at Het Steen
new.desc: Antwerp's oldest building, a 13th-century castle gate, once served as a prison and now houses the visitor centre. On the bridge stands the giant Lange Wapper, the trickster of local folklore.
new.tip: The building and its riverside terrace are free; only the 'Antwerp Story' exhibition needs a ticket. Browse the shop for local specialities.

new.title: Visit Rubens' friend at the Snijders&Rockoxhuis
new.desc: Two neighbouring houses: that of Nicolaas Rockox, eight times mayor and friend of Rubens, and that of the animal painter Frans Snijders. Works by Snijders, Jordaens, Van Dyck and Rubens hang in rooms that still feel lived in.
new.tip: Don't miss the reconstructed 17th-century garden with orange trees, which you can only reach through the museum.

new.title: Climb among the giant buoys of the Boeienweide
new.desc: On Linkeroever, a riverside meadow doubles as an open-air maritime museum: huge buoys, anchors and old cannons scattered on the grass, with a playground in between and the skyline across the Schelde.
new.tip: Walk out of the Sint-Annatunnel and turn right along the river; combine it with a cone of fries on the square at the tunnel exit.

new.title: Follow the emigrants at the Red Star Line Museum
new.desc: From these warehouses, millions of Europeans boarded ships for America, among them a young Irving Berlin; Albert Einstein also sailed the line. The museum tells their stories in the original buildings.
new.tip: Finish by climbing the funnel-shaped tower for a sweeping view over the docks and the port.
new.q: Red Star Line Museum Montevideostraat Antwerpen

new.title: Walk the line of old port cranes
new.desc: Along the Schelde quays between the MAS and the Red Star Line Museum stands a row of historic harbour cranes, kept as part of the MAS collection as a reminder of when the port was right in town.
new.tip: Go at golden hour and photograph them against the river; don't climb them and stay back from the quay edge.

new.title: Look up at the steel sails of the courthouse
new.desc: Richard Rogers' Justitiepaleis at the end of the Leien crowns its courtrooms with stainless steel roofs shaped like sails or butterfly wings, a landmark of Nieuw Zuid.
new.tip: Peek into the vast light-filled entrance hall; the inner gardens can only be seen through the glass.

new.title: Find Nello and Patrasche in Hoboken
new.desc: Hoboken has long been seen as the home of the boy and his dog from 'A Dog of Flanders', the story Japanese and Korean visitors know by heart. A bronze statue stands on Kapelstraat, and locals say the pair lie buried near the Kioskplaats.
new.tip: Cycle the 7 km from the Grote Markt or take the tram; look for 'Nello and Patrasche' chocolates at the bakery on the Kioskplaats.

new.title: Spot the okapi at the Egyptian temple
new.desc: Opened in 1843 right next to Centraal station, Antwerp Zoo is one of the oldest in the world, and its 19th-century buildings, including an Egyptian temple and a Moorish temple, are protected monuments. It was the first zoo ever to show an okapi.
new.tip: Take time for the 1897 winter garden and the aquarium building; the zoo is as much an architecture walk as an animal park.

new.title: Order a bolleke at Den Engel
new.desc: On the corner of the Grote Markt, Den Engel is the most famous traditional café in town: wood panelling, regulars at the bar and a De Koninck in its round glass.
new.tip: Sit inside rather than on the terrace to hear the Antwerp dialect at the bar.
new.q: Café Den Engel Grote Markt Antwerpen

new.title: Taste jenever at De Vagant
new.desc: This old-fashioned café specialises in jenever, the juniper spirit of the Low Countries, with a list of around 300 kinds, from young and grainy to aged and fruity.
new.tip: Ask the bartender for a tasting of a 'jonge' and an 'oude' side by side; the shop across the street sells bottles to take home.

new.title: Dance to the Decap organ at Café Beveren
new.desc: A tiny brown café near the river whose star is a giant, brightly painted Decap dance organ that plays at the drop of a coin; regulars start dancing between the tables.
new.tip: Bring some change for the organ and go late on a weekend evening, when the place is at its liveliest.

new.title: Drink a Trappist among the saints at Het Elfde Gebod
new.desc: The 'Eleventh Commandment' sits in the shadow of the cathedral and is crammed from floor to ceiling with church statues and saints, a strange and wonderful setting for a Belgian abbey beer.
new.tip: It is busy at peak times; go mid-afternoon on a weekday to get a seat inside.

new.title: Join the regulars at 't Oud Arsenaal
new.desc: A brown café from the 1920s with its original interior, old wallpaper and a stove, beloved by locals for its well-kept beer list and unhurried atmosphere.
new.tip: Ask for the beer of the month on the board and settle in at a table by the window.

new.title: Dine in the wings of the Bourla
new.desc: Café Bourla occupies part of the 19th-century Bourla theatre on the Graanmarkt, serving Belgian and French classics in a grand setting at fair prices.
new.tip: Book a table before a show at the theatre next door, or come for a late lunch on a quiet weekday.

new.title: Eat fries with a skyline view on Linkeroever
new.desc: Right where the Sint-Annatunnel comes up on the left bank, Frituur LO serves fries that locals cross the river for, with the best view of the old town just a few steps away.
new.tip: Take your cone to the riverside walk or the Boeienweide and eat looking back at the cathedral.
new.q: Frituur LO Frederik van Eedenplein Antwerpen

new.title: Share mezze by the MAS at Napos
new.desc: A Middle Eastern grill on the quay next to the MAS, popular for its colourful mezze and grilled meats after a museum visit on Eilandje.
new.tip: Order a selection of mezze for the table and add one grill dish; reserve on weekend evenings.

new.title: Grab a cruffin at Bakkerij Funk
new.desc: A neighbourhood bakery in Het Zuid with a seasonal menu, known for its sourdough loaves, almond croissants and pistachio cruffins.
new.tip: Go early, as the cruffins sell out; eat yours on the steps of the KMSKA a few streets away.

new.title: Eat Yiddish home cooking at Hoffy's
new.desc: A kosher restaurant in the diamond quarter run by three brothers, serving the Ashkenazi dishes of the neighbourhood's Jewish community, a short walk from Centraal station.
new.tip: It is closed on Shabbat (Friday evening and Saturday); come for lunch on a weekday and ask what is homemade that day.

new.title: Slow down over a tajine at El Warda
new.desc: A Moroccan restaurant near the Draakplaats in Zurenborg, recommended for its slow-cooked halal tajines and generous dishes made for sharing.
new.tip: Combine it with an evening walk past the Art Nouveau facades of Zurenborg; go with friends and order several tajines for the table.

new.title: Start the day with pancakes at Barchel
new.desc: A breakfast spot on Van Breestraat, close to the Stadspark, that locals recommend above all for its pancakes.
new.tip: Pair it with a morning loop around the Stadspark, which is pleasantly free of tourists before noon.

new.title: Go underground into the Ruien
new.desc: The Ruien are the city's old canals, covered over the centuries and turned into a network of vaults, sluices and tunnels under the old town. A guided walk takes you through them in a protective suit.
new.tip: Book a time slot online in advance; tours start from the Ruihuis on Suikerrui and are not suitable for young children.

new.title: Hunt for Madonnas on street corners
new.desc: More than 160 statues of the Virgin Mary keep watch from the corners of buildings in the old centre, many of them put up by neighbours or guilds centuries ago.
new.tip: Start at the Ossenmarkt, which has several, and keep looking up as you walk towards the cathedral; count how many you find.

new.title: Dig for treasure on Kloosterstraat
new.desc: Locals skip the Meir and shop here instead: a long street of vintage, antiques, design and interior shops running from the Sint-Andries quarter towards Het Zuid.
new.tip: Go on a Sunday afternoon, when many shops are open and the street is at its most relaxed.

new.title: Take the boat to Sint-Anneke beach
new.desc: Across the river on Linkeroever, a sandy city beach on the Schelde has been a summer escape for Antwerpenaren for a century, lined with cafés and restaurants serving mussels and fries.
new.tip: The waterbus from Steenplein gets you there in about ten minutes. Swimming in the river is forbidden; the open-air pool by the mill is the place for a dip.

new.title: Cross the Parkbrug to Park Spoor Noord
new.desc: The Parkbrug carries walkers and cyclists from Eilandje over the Italiëlei into Park Spoor Noord, a former railway yard turned into a vast lawn with sports fields, a skate area and free public barbecues.
new.tip: On a sunny evening bring your own food and charcoal and claim one of the barbecues; there are no toilets in the park.

new.title: Walk around the Fort van Merksem
new.desc: Built in 1876 as part of Antwerp's ring of forts and blown up in 1914, the fort in Merksem is now a green domain with moats, sports fields and paths between allotments.
new.tip: Follow the cycle and walking path behind the fort between the allotment gardens; afterwards wander along the Bredabaan, one of Belgium's longest shopping streets.

new.title: Board a vintage tram in Berchem
new.desc: In the old Groenenhoek tram depot from 1912, the Vlaams Tram- en Autobusmuseum keeps around 70 historic trams and buses, including the only surviving gyrobus in the world.
new.tip: It only opens on weekend afternoons in the warm season; take tram 4 or 9 to Berchem Groenenhoek.
new.q: Vlaams Tram- en Autobusmuseum Diksmuidelaan Berchem

new.title: Catch a show at De Roma in Borgerhout
new.desc: A 1928 picture palace on the Turnhoutsebaan, once the biggest cinema in Antwerp and later a rock venue, was saved and restored by hundreds of volunteers and is now a beloved concert and theatre hall.
new.tip: Check the programme for a concert, film or comedy night, then eat on the Turnhoutsebaan beforehand.

new.title: Row, stroll or see a show in the Rivierenhof
new.desc: Deurne's Rivierenhof is the largest park in the city: ponds, the meandering Schijn river, rose gardens, an arboretum, an 18th-century castle and the open-air theatre OLT Rivierenhof, which hosts concerts all summer.
new.tip: Tram 10 stops at Deurne Venneborg. In summer, book an evening concert at the open-air theatre and picnic beforehand.

new.title: Swim in the natural pond at Boekenberg
new.desc: Boekenbergpark in Deurne opened Belgium's first ecological swimming pond in 2007, cleaned by plants instead of chlorine, in a romantic park with a ruin tower and grottoes.
new.tip: The pond is only open in the summer season; on hot days arrive early, as the number of swimmers is limited.

new.title: Sing along with The Great Old at the Bosuil
new.desc: Royal Antwerp FC, Belgium's oldest club and known as 'The Great Old', has played at the Bosuil stadium in Deurne since 1923. A home match is a loud, red-and-white crash course in local pride.
new.tip: Buy tickets through the club in advance and take the tram out early to soak up the atmosphere in the cafés around the stadium.

new.title: Window-shop for diamonds on Pelikaanstraat
new.desc: Next to the station, the streets of the diamond quarter are lined with jewellers' windows; most of the world's rough diamonds pass through the offices around here.
new.tip: Many shops close on Saturday for Shabbat. If you are buying, bargaining is normal here, unlike almost anywhere else in Belgium.

fix.problem: The tip says to go up near sunset, but the free rooftop and boulevard are only accessible during opening hours (closed on Mondays); for much of the year sunset falls after closing.
fix.suggestion: Change the tip to 'Go up late in the afternoon' and mention that the rooftop is free during opening hours and closed on Mondays.

fix.problem: Middelheimmuseum is on Middelheimlaan in Wilrijk, not in Zuid or Berchem; the area key 'zuid' (Zuid & Berchem) is the closest fit but the desc does not say where it is.
fix.suggestion: Keep area 'zuid' but mention Wilrijk in the desc or tip (e.g. 'on the southern edge of the city in Wilrijk').
